title: Heterogeneous memory budgeting blueprint for mixed workloads
creator: Maya Chen
description: Problem: Serving heterogeneous inference mixes (short chat, long-context retrieval, embedding batches) causes unpredictable KV cache pressure and spike eviction/activation churn. Current single-headroom heuristic leads to either wasted idle memory or tail latency regressions during bursts. Goal: define and validate a heterogeneous memory budgeting blueprint that simultaneously accounts for immutable weight residency, dynamic KV cache growth, activation stack needs for peak batched sequences, and a micro-reserve for preemption and emergency allocation. Outcome: a set of simple-to-evaluate heuristics and a proof-of-concept allocator that reduces KV-eviction frequency by >= 40% on mixed workloads while keeping p99 latency within SLOs and limiting GPU OOMs to zero in stress tests.
acceptance_criteria: Blueprint doc with formulas for weight/KV/activation partitioning and headroom policy approved by infra and runtime leads
Simulator runs demonstrating >=40% reduction in KV eviction events for representative mixes (chat:60%, retrieval:25%, embed:15%)
Prototype allocator integrated into staging runtime with opt-in flag; monitors show p99 latency impact <= +5% and no OOMs in 48h soak
Migration guide and config knobs documented in Console for Dedicated and Private deployments

design_notes: We propose a three-band memory model: (1) Weight floor = model weights and reserved kernels, (2) KV waterline = expected KV steady-state with 95th-percentile buffer, (3) Activation buffer = max expected transient activation peak per-batch + micro-reserve (2-5% of GPU mem) for preemption handling.

Soft vs hard guardrails: soft waterline triggers proactive lightweight eviction (LRU with async flush) and batching throttling; hard guardrail enforces admission-control and spills to host memory only for activations, not weights.

Inter-GPU spillover concept: allow low-priority KV shards to be evicted and reconstructed from peer replicas (metadata index) instead of immediate recompute to save memory at cost of slight latency increase for those tokens.
Headroom phasing: when utilization trending up, gradually increase micro-reserve and ramp down batching aggressiveness; when trending down, reclaim and re-enable aggressive batching.
Telemetry signals: introduce KV_growth_rate, activation_peak_ratio, eviction_throttle_count as signals used by controller to decide phase transitions.
tradeoffs: Aggressive micro-reserve increases idle memory and cost but reduces OOM risk and eviction churn.
Inter-GPU spill increases complexity (replication metadata) and may add tail latency for evicted KV rehydration.
Spill-to-host for activations reduces GPU pressure but introduces PCIe overhead; acceptable only for low-priority backfills.
Stricter admission-control reduces throughput for high-concurrency tenants; consider tenant-level QoS tiers.
experiments_plan: Baseline collection: run 72h traces on current production heuristic (sampled) and extract histograms - dataset: prod-sample-2026-02
Simulator matrix: run 20 workload mixes varying short/long/embedding ratios, seq lengths, and burstiness; metric: eviction_rate, p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput
A/B staging: deploy prototype allocator behind opt-in flag for 10% of requests; monitor for regressions and OOMs
Stress test: synthetic spike tests with 3x arrival rate for 10 minutes to validate preemption behavior
risks_and_mitigations: Risk: Micro-reserve size mis-tuned causing wasted capacity. Mitigation: auto-tune using rolling window and revert threshold if utilization drops >10% without eviction improvements.
Risk: New admission-control impacts high-priority tenants. Mitigation: tenant QoS labels and conservative canary rollout with manual overrides.
Risk: Spill-to-peer introduces consistency bugs. Mitigation: small PoC with read-only KV shards and end-to-end validation harness before enabling writes.
